prompt:
A reinforcement-learning agent learns to control a simulated physical
system on a hexagonal grid. Learning works but needs tens of millions of
environment steps; the simulator is the bottleneck. Standard tricks tried:
frame skipping, prioritised replay, reward shaping, curriculum. Want a
different angle on sample efficiency.

Incorporate ideas from Pancasila Values in Education (Social Sciences > Social Sciences > Education > Pancasila Values in Education) into your approach.
proposal:
## Framing: five Pancasila principles as five design lenses

Pancasila isn't just a values list — in Indonesian education practice it's operationalized as a set of *process commitments*: pool resources (gotong royong), resolve disagreement through deliberation rather than domination (musyawarah mufakat), distribute effort/benefit fairly (keadilan sosial), unify diverse parts under one shared structure without erasing their differences (persatuan/Bhinneka Tunggal Ika), and let a transcendent/guiding order inform action rather than starting from nothing (Ketuhanan). Read that way, each principle maps cleanly onto a *known but underused* RL technique — and none of them overlap with frame-skip/PER/reward-shaping/curriculum, which is the "different angle" you asked for.

None of these five are individually novel in isolation — the novelty is in using the values framework to force you to combine all five into one coherent pipeline rather than bolting on one trick.

## 1. Ketuhanan → bake in structure instead of learning it from scratch

**Technique: hex-grid equivariant architecture.** A hexagonal grid has a D6 symmetry group (6-fold rotation + reflection). If your policy/value network doesn't know this, it has to independently learn "rotated state X behaves like state Y" from data, N times over. A group-equivariant network (or even just D6 data augmentation at training time) collapses that redundancy for free. This is usually the single biggest unclaimed win in your list of tricks tried — none of frame-skip/PER/reward-shaping/curriculum touch the symmetry structure at all. Expect a multiplicative reduction (roughly the size of the symmetry orbit, up to ~12x for D6) in effective samples needed, because every real transition now teaches the network about 12 equivalent transitions.

## 2. Gotong royong → stop paying the simulator for every gradient step

**Technique: learned world model + imagined rollouts (Dyna/MuZero/Dreamer-style).** The simulator is the bottleneck, so stop treating it as the only source of experience. Train a learned dynamics model on real (hex-state, action, next-state, reward) tuples, then generate the bulk of training rollouts by "imagining" forward through the model instead of stepping the real simulator. Real steps become a shared resource the whole training process draws from collectively, rather than something re-paid for every rollout — the "mutual cooperation" framing is literal here: the model pools everyone's real experience into a resource cheap rollouts can draw from. This is where model-based methods typically report 10–100x reductions in real environment steps vs. model-free baselines.

## 3. Musyawarah mufakat → let disagreement decide where the simulator gets spent

**Technique: ensemble-disagreement-driven active data collection.** Train an ensemble (5–10 members) of the world model above. Where ensemble members disagree strongly on predicted next-state/reward, that's a region of real uncertainty — send *those* states to the real simulator; where they agree, trust the imagined rollout. This turns your scarce simulator budget into a deliberation process — you spend real compute resolving disagreement, not confirming what's already known (this is the Plan2Explore / bootstrapped-uncertainty family of methods, just re-motivated).

## 4. Keadilan sosial → spend the simulator budget equitably, not just where reward is high

**Technique: count-based/archive coverage alongside disagreement.** Reward-following exploration (and most curricula) concentrate simulator budget near high-reward regions of the hex grid, starving rarely-visited-but-structurally-important cells (e.g., corners, boundary conditions, rare piece configurations). Maintain a per-cell (or per-region) visitation archive (Go-Explore style) and mix a coverage-equity term into your acquisition function alongside disagreement: spend some fixed fraction of the real-simulator budget on the least-visited regions regardless of reward. This catches the systematic blind spots that reward-shaping and PER structurally can't — they're both reward-weighted by design.

## 5. Persatuan / Bhinneka Tunggal Ika → one shared backbone across the whole curriculum

**Technique: unify representation across curriculum stages instead of resetting it.** If your curriculum trains successive stages as semi-independent phases, you're likely discarding representational learning at each transition. Keep one shared equivariant encoder/world-model backbone across *all* curriculum stages (diverse tasks, one shared structure — the Bhinneka Tunggal Ika move) and only let stage-specific heads vary. Early-stage simulator steps then keep paying dividends in later stages instead of the sample count effectively resetting per stage.

## Optional 6th lens: kemanusiaan yang adil dan beradab → bootstrap from a small human demo set

If any expert or scripted trajectories exist (even a few dozen), use them to pretrain the world model and initialize the policy (DQfD/R2D3-style) before online collection starts. This front-loads "wisdom" the agent would otherwise burn early random-exploration steps rediscovering, and pairs naturally with #2 since demos also warm-start the world model.

## Net pipeline

Symmetry-equivariant world model (1), trained from real transitions and demos (6), generating the bulk of rollouts via imagination (2), with real simulator calls allocated by an ensemble-disagreement + visitation-equity acquisition function (3+4), sharing one backbone across curriculum stages (5).

This is a genuinely different axis from what you've tried — all four prior tricks (frame skip, PER, reward shaping, curriculum) optimize *how you use each simulator step*; this pipeline instead reduces *how many simulator steps you need in the first place*, which is where the 10x+ gains typically live once you've already exhausted the first category.

Want me to sketch the acquisition function (disagreement + coverage-equity term) more concretely, or scope this as a phased experiment plan?
